questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted it to be different from Denmark so I wanted to go to some of the southern states in the US. Florida was cheaper than California so that's why i chose USF.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Amazing experience, it was the best five months of my life. Would recommend it everyone who has the opportunity to go.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy since a lot of people on campus are ready to help you with finding your school ID, house keys, and where to go. There was also people ready to help with any questions you may have.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I arrived at the wrong building and a very nice girl offered to drive me to the housing location since it was a long walk and super hot outside. I met some people at the key pickup place that helped me navigate to my housing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: We had an orientation just for exchange students which gave a lot of useful information. However it would have been nice to get some information about the area. I found out later that one area outside USF is very unsafe and it's not recommended to walk there, and that would have been nice to know from the start.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Apartment style: Students have their own room or share with roommate and bathrooms and kitchen/living room is shared only by roommates.
Suite style: Students share a bedroom with a roommate and bathrooms are shared only by suite-mates. Common kitchen area.
Traditional style: Students share a bedroom with a roommate and a community bathroom with their floormates. Common kitchen area.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: They had a lot of different meal plans but I would recommend to get the BullBlock 150. The unlimited meal plan is not worth it according to the students i talked to who had it. I had the BullBlock 50 which was a bit too small since a lot of socializing takes place at the dining hall, and I ended up having to get meal swipes from my friends.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The dorms are not very new or clean but it is definitely part of the college experience. I wouldn't have done it any different. I would also recommend living on campus, since the few exchange students that lived off campus has some issues with their leases and they were more isolated and less social.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some of the dorms need some renovations soon but I liked how easy it was to have a social life when living in an apartment-style dorm. It seemed like they put all the exchange students in apartment or suite-style dorms which did make it easier to socialize.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was very easy to register as soon as you figured out how to and you know right away if you got a spot on the course.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When the registration opens you can go into your OASIS account (which is like KU selvbetjening) and type in the course code for the course you want and press submit. Then you are registered right away. The course code can be found on the schedule search for the current semester, where you can also see what time of day the course lectures are and how many spots are available.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We went over the course registration at the exchange orientation.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Quite successful, however, some of the courses I put on my application for pre-approval was not taught in my semester so I had to re-apply for pre-approval.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You don't have to find your final courses on the first day of class. I ended up registering for 2 more courses than necessary and then dropping the classes I didn't find interesting and adding another one. You can also register for courses in the add/drop week even though you didn't attend the first day of class.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was fine for the most part but it takes some time to adjust to the American school system.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level is for the most part was lower than at UCPH. Even the ones they called "high level courses" where they  warned us about the amount of studying required was not very challenging and didn't really require that much studying. For the most part I just paid attention during the lectures and did my homework, and I got B's and A's.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The exams required a lot less independent thinking and much more that you remember a bunch of the material from the lecture slides. I had to get used to studying to remember and not necessarily to understand. 
In my courses we mostly had 75 minute lectures, and then a lot of quizzes and a few assignments. The amount of quizzes are obviously higher than UCPH and the assignments were usually less time consuming than what I am used to.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Molecular Microbiology
Molecular Biology of the Gene
Nutrition and Disease
Introduction to Earth Science

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Molecular Microbiology was a great course. The professor was great at teaching and the work load was also fitting. If you've taken any microbiology courses at home this one will build on that knowledge.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The TOEFL English test for 2000 DKK and the cost of setting up my room and getting cleaning supplies for the apartment. I also had a spontaneous trip that required a plane ticket.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: You can get a pretty cheap phone plan through Mint Mobile with call, texts and data which is what most exchange students did (it is cheaper than going to Target/Walmart to get one). A lot of food was more expensive than expected like meat and fruit, but that wouldn't have been an issue if I had a bigger meal plan.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have everything from dance and tennis to video games and cooking.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you're really good at a sport you can go to try-outs for sport clubs and maybe join a team. That is one way to make friends and be part of a team, and that way you also have the opportunity to compete outside USF.
If you want to play a sport for fun you can join an intermural sport team. You also have trainings and competitions but only at USF against other intermural teams.
They obviously also have football, basketball, volleyball and soccer teams where you can get free student tickets to go watch the games. 
If you are interested in joining any clubs they have quite a few events where you can hear all about them and other social events. USF have patio Tuesdays (first Tuesday every month) which is just a social event, and Bulls Nite Out every other Friday where they stream movies and have some activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I personally found a lot of friends at the Bulls Nite Out events and the tailgate parties before football games. All the social event are on the app BullsConnect where you can read about them and see when and where, and there is a lot every day of the week. Just go to as many of them as you like and talk to people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Miami, Cocoa Beach, Clearwater Beach, Crystal River, Lettuce Lake Park, Rainbow River Springs, Downtown Tampa, Orlando and the whole Disney area (Disney Springs), Universal Studios and Busch Gardens.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy since I knew the language and the culture is somewhat similar to Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you initiate a conversation they are all super easy to talk to and will ask a lot of questions. Sometimes they will also start the conversation. Make plans with them to keep in touch and you will likely become friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Metal detectors at every event and no-bag policies.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and how they are willing to take in foreign students. Everybody I met were so nice to me and I even got invited home at Thanksgiving.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Trust the process, everything will work out and you will figure everything out little by little. Be open minded to all the people you meet and you will definitely make friends. Try new things and don't be scared to push some of your limits.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take advantage of the Bull Runner busses on campus - you can use them for free if you show them your USF ID. Also the busses outside campus is free if you show them your ID. The busses are useful when you have to go to Target or Walmart the first day to get all your stuff for your room. The fifth floor of the library is the best one for a quiet study with new seating and the whole floor is quiet.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: How many amazing people I have met and to try the college experience in America in the American school system.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To adjust to their school system since the exams were quite different from those at UCPH and I needed to study differently than I was used to. Also, it felt lonely in the beginning when you don't know a lot of people yet. I was the only Danish student and everyone was hanging out with people from their own country in the beginning so I went to a lot of events on my own.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
